provisions.document: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI)
provisions.article_or_section: Article 9(1)-(9) (Chapter III, Section 2) – Risk management system
provisions.exact_text: A risk management system shall be established, implemented, documented and maintained in relation to high-risk AI systems.
provisions.provision_summary: Providers must run a documented, continuous and iterative risk management process across the whole lifecycle of a high-risk AI system. It covers identifying and analysing known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, estimating risks under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse, evaluating risks from post-market monitoring data, and adopting targeted mitigation measures so that residual risk is judged acceptable.
provisions.responsible_party: AI provider (of high-risk AI systems)
provisions.applicability_status: Legally adopted but not yet applicable
provisions.implementation_notes: QUALIFIER: legislative obligation. Not assessed: legislative obligation, not a policy commitment. Timing is recorded in applicability_status. Check separately whether harmonised standards supporting this article have been published. APPLICABILITY: from 2 Dec 2027 (Art. 6(2)/Annex III systems) or 2 Aug 2028 (Art. 6(1)/Annex I systems), per Art. 113 as amended. Provider duty; not applicable to deployers or to AI systems that are not high-risk.
provisions.enforcement_mechanism: Art. 16(a) (cons. p. 28; OJ p. 62) obliges providers to ensure compliance with Chapter III Section 2 (Arts 8-15). Non-compliance with Art. 16 provider obligations is subject to fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher (Art. 99(4)(a), cons. p. 116; OJ p. 115; unchanged by 2026/1744). Ex ante conformity assessment (Art. 43, cons. p. 53); market surveillance (Art. 74, cons. p. 91) and procedure for AI systems presenting a risk (Art. 79, cons. p. 104).
provisions.source_reference: Consolidated text (27.07.2026): https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/2026-07-27/eng/pdf (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/2026-07-27); Original act: OJ L, 2024/1689, 12.7.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj; Amending act: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of 8 July 2026, OJ L, 2026/1744, 24.7.2026, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj
provisions.verification_notes: Binding requirement. The article is phrased in the passive voice; the duty-holder (provider) is established through Art. 16(a) and the reference to 'providers' in Art. 9(9). OVERLAP: Art. 9(6)-(8) (OJ p. 57) also imposes testing duties (testing against prior defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds, before market placement) that fit Safety and Testing; coded here under Risk Assessment only, to avoid double counting, with the testing element noted. Art. 9(10) (integration with risk procedures under other Union law, e.g. financial services) is outside the coded range. No amendment marker (M1) appears in Art. 9 of the consolidated text; wording unchanged. APPLICATION DATE: as amended by Reg. (EU) 2026/1744, Art. 113 (cons. p. 128) applies Chapter III high-risk obligations from 2 Dec 2027 for systems classified under Art. 6(2) and Annex III, and from 2 Aug 2028 for systems classified under Art. 6(1) and Annex I (originally 2 Aug 2026 and 2 Aug 2027 respectively). As of Nov 2026 the obligation is binding law but not yet applicable. provisions.document: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI)
provisions.article_or_section: Article 10(1)-(4), (6) (Chapter III, Section 2) – Data and data governance; read with Article 4a(1)
provisions.exact_text: Training, validation and testing data sets shall be subject to data governance and management practices appropriate for the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system.
provisions.provision_summary: High-risk AI systems trained on data must be developed using training, validation and testing data sets that meet quality criteria. Data governance practices must cover design choices, data origin and collection, preparation steps such as labelling and cleaning, assumptions, the suitability of the data, examination for possible biases with measures to detect, prevent and mitigate them, and the identification of data gaps. Data sets must be relevant, sufficiently representative, as error-free and complete as possible, and suited to the setting in which the system is intended to be used.
provisions.responsible_party: AI provider (of high-risk AI systems)
provisions.applicability_status: Legally adopted but not yet applicable
provisions.implementation_notes: QUALIFIER: legislative obligation. Not assessed: legislative obligation, not a policy commitment. Timing is recorded in applicability_status. Check separately whether harmonised standards supporting this article have been published. APPLICABILITY: from 2 Dec 2027 (Art. 6(2)/Annex III systems) or 2 Aug 2028 (Art. 6(1)/Annex I systems), per Art. 113 as amended. Provider duty; not applicable to AI systems that are not high-risk (Art. 4a(2) permission does extend to them).
provisions.enforcement_mechanism: Art. 16(a) (cons. p. 28; OJ p. 62) obliges providers to ensure compliance with Chapter III Section 2 (Arts 8-15). Non-compliance with Art. 16 provider obligations is subject to fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher (Art. 99(4)(a), cons. p. 116; OJ p. 115; unchanged by 2026/1744). Ex ante conformity assessment (Art. 43, cons. p. 53); market surveillance (Art. 74, cons. p. 91) and procedure for AI systems presenting a risk (Art. 79, cons. p. 104).
provisions.source_reference: Consolidated text (27.07.2026): https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/2026-07-27/eng/pdf (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/2026-07-27); Original act: OJ L, 2024/1689, 12.7.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj; Amending act: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of 8 July 2026, OJ L, 2026/1744, 24.7.2026, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj
provisions.verification_notes: CODING DECISION: Art. 10 is fundamentally a data governance provision, even though some of its requirements relate to risk mitigation. It is coded under Risk Assessment for now because its core operative elements, bias examination (Art. 10(2)(f)), bias detection, prevention and mitigation (Art. 10(2)(g)) and identification of data gaps (Art. 10(2)(h)), are risk identification and mitigation functions. Secondary fit: Safety and Testing (quality of testing data sets). Single record, no double count. FUTURE CODEBOOK: candidate for a sixth dimension, Data Governance. AMENDMENT: Reg. (EU) 2026/1744 amended Art. 10(1) (M1 marker) so the quality criteria now refer to paras 2, 3 and 4 and to Art. 4a(1) instead of paras 2 to 5. It also deleted Art. 10(5) and moved the special-category data rule into new Art. 4a (cons. p. 12). The coded exact_text (opening of Art. 10(2)) appears unamended. PERMISSION vs OBLIGATION: Art. 4a(1) PERMITS providers of high-risk AI systems, exceptionally and where strictly necessary, to process special categories of personal data for the bias detection and correction required by Art. 10(2)(f)-(g), subject to cumulative safeguards. Art. 4a(2) extends that permission to providers and deployers of other AI systems and models and to deployers of high-risk systems, and expressly states that it does not create any obligation to conduct bias detection and correction. So the DUTY to examine and mitigate bias comes from Art. 10(2)(f)-(g) and binds high-risk providers only, while Art. 4a is an enabling permission, not an obligation, and is not coded as a separate mandatory record. Must be read alongside the GDPR (Art. 1(2)(g) as amended is without prejudice to Art. 4a). APPLICATION DATE: as amended by Reg. (EU) 2026/1744, Art. 113 (cons. p. 128) applies Chapter III high-risk obligations from 2 Dec 2027 for systems classified under Art. 6(2) and Annex III, and from 2 Aug 2028 for systems classified under Art. 6(1) and Annex I (originally 2 Aug 2026 and 2 Aug 2027 respectively). As of Nov 2026 the obligation is binding law but not yet applicable. provisions.document: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI)
provisions.article_or_section: Article 13(1)-(3) (Chapter III, Section 2) – Transparency and provision of information to deployers
provisions.exact_text: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way as to ensure that their operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret a system’s output and use it appropriately.
provisions.provision_summary: High-risk AI systems must be transparent enough for deployers to interpret their outputs and use them appropriately. They must come with instructions for use giving concise, complete, correct and clear information. At minimum this includes the provider's identity, the system's intended purpose, its capabilities and limitations, its accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity levels, foreseeable risk circumstances, any capabilities for explaining outputs, human oversight measures, maintenance needs and log-handling mechanisms.
provisions.responsible_party: AI provider (information duty owed to deployers)
provisions.applicability_status: Legally adopted but not yet applicable
provisions.implementation_notes: QUALIFIER: legislative obligation. Not assessed: legislative obligation, not a policy commitment. Timing is recorded in applicability_status. Check separately whether harmonised standards supporting this article have been published. APPLICABILITY: from 2 Dec 2027 (Art. 6(2)/Annex III systems) or 2 Aug 2028 (Art. 6(1)/Annex I systems), per Art. 113 as amended. Provider duty owed to deployers; not applicable to AI systems that are not high-risk (compare Art. 50).
provisions.enforcement_mechanism: Art. 16(a) (cons. p. 28; OJ p. 62) obliges providers to ensure compliance with Chapter III Section 2 (Arts 8-15). Non-compliance with Art. 16 provider obligations is subject to fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher (Art. 99(4)(a), cons. p. 116; OJ p. 115; unchanged by 2026/1744). Ex ante conformity assessment (Art. 43, cons. p. 53); market surveillance (Art. 74, cons. p. 91) and procedure for AI systems presenting a risk (Art. 79, cons. p. 104). Deployers must use systems in accordance with the instructions for use (Art. 26(1); Art. 26 begins cons. p. 37), with deployer breaches finable under Art. 99(4)(e).
provisions.source_reference: Consolidated text (27.07.2026): https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/2026-07-27/eng/pdf (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/2026-07-27); Original act: OJ L, 2024/1689, 12.7.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj; Amending act: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of 8 July 2026, OJ L, 2026/1744, 24.7.2026, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj
provisions.verification_notes: Binding requirement. Scope is B2B transparency (provider to deployer), not public disclosure; do not equate with general 'explainability to the public'. Art. 13(3)(b)(iv) requires explanation-relevant information only 'where applicable', so explainability is conditional rather than absolute. Cross-references: Art. 15 (accuracy metrics declared in instructions, Art. 15(3)), Art. 14 (oversight measures, Art. 13(3)(d)), Art. 12 (logs, Art. 13(3)(f)). Separate from Art. 50 transparency obligations (candidate for a later record). No M1 marker in Art. 13; wording unchanged. APPLICATION DATE: as amended by Reg. (EU) 2026/1744, Art. 113 (cons. p. 128) applies Chapter III high-risk obligations from 2 Dec 2027 for systems classified under Art. 6(2) and Annex III, and from 2 Aug 2028 for systems classified under Art. 6(1) and Annex I (originally 2 Aug 2026 and 2 Aug 2027 respectively). As of Nov 2026 the obligation is binding law but not yet applicable. provisions.document: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI)
provisions.article_or_section: Article 14(1)-(4) (Chapter III, Section 2) – Human oversight
provisions.exact_text: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which they are in use.
provisions.provision_summary: High-risk AI systems must be designed so that natural persons can effectively oversee them while in use, with the aim of preventing or minimising risks to health, safety or fundamental rights. Oversight measures must be proportionate to risk, autonomy and context, and may be built in by the provider or identified by the provider for the deployer to implement. Overseers must be able to understand the system's limitations, stay aware of automation bias, interpret outputs, decide not to use or override the output, and stop the system safely.
provisions.responsible_party: AI provider (design obligation); AI deployer (implementation, via Art. 26(2))
provisions.applicability_status: Legally adopted but not yet applicable
provisions.implementation_notes: QUALIFIER: legislative obligation. Not assessed: legislative obligation, not a policy commitment. Timing is recorded in applicability_status. Check separately whether harmonised standards supporting this article have been published. APPLICABILITY: from 2 Dec 2027 (Art. 6(2)/Annex III systems) or 2 Aug 2028 (Art. 6(1)/Annex I systems), per Art. 113 as amended. Provider design duty; deployer duty arises under Art. 26(2); not applicable to AI systems that are not high-risk.
provisions.enforcement_mechanism: Art. 16(a) (cons. p. 28; OJ p. 62) obliges providers to ensure compliance with Chapter III Section 2 (Arts 8-15). Non-compliance with Art. 16 provider obligations is subject to fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher (Art. 99(4)(a), cons. p. 116; OJ p. 115; unchanged by 2026/1744). Ex ante conformity assessment (Art. 43, cons. p. 53); market surveillance (Art. 74, cons. p. 91) and procedure for AI systems presenting a risk (Art. 79, cons. p. 104). Deployers must assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority (Art. 26(2); Art. 26 begins cons. p. 37, OJ p. 68 for para. 2; unchanged by 2026/1744); breach finable under Art. 99(4)(e).
provisions.source_reference: Consolidated text (27.07.2026): https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/2026-07-27/eng/pdf (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/2026-07-27); Original act: OJ L, 2024/1689, 12.7.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj; Amending act: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of 8 July 2026, OJ L, 2026/1744, 24.7.2026, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj
provisions.verification_notes: Binding requirement. Shared responsibility: Art. 14 itself places design duties on the provider (Art. 14(3)(a)-(b)), while the duty to actually staff oversight sits with deployers under Art. 26(2). Responsible party is therefore recorded as two actors; for responsibility analysis, count the provider as the primary duty-holder for this record and note Art. 26(2) as a possible separate deployer record. Classified as Accountability (human oversight is listed under that dimension in the codebook), although its stated aim (Art. 14(2)) is risk prevention, so there is a secondary link to Risk Assessment. The coded range is Art. 14(1)-(4); para. 5 (biometric two-person verification) appears only in applicability. No M1 marker in Art. 14; wording unchanged. APPLICATION DATE: as amended by Reg. (EU) 2026/1744, Art. 113 (cons. p. 128) applies Chapter III high-risk obligations from 2 Dec 2027 for systems classified under Art. 6(2) and Annex III, and from 2 Aug 2028 for systems classified under Art. 6(1) and Annex I (originally 2 Aug 2026 and 2 Aug 2027 respectively). As of Nov 2026 the obligation is binding law but not yet applicable. provisions.document: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI)
provisions.article_or_section: Article 15(1), (3)-(5) (Chapter III, Section 2) – Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity
provisions.exact_text: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way that they achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity, and that they perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle.
provisions.provision_summary: High-risk AI systems must achieve appropriate accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity and keep performing consistently throughout their lifecycle. They must be resilient to errors, faults and inconsistencies (possibly through redundancy or fail-safe plans), manage feedback loops in systems that keep learning, and resist attacks that exploit vulnerabilities. This includes, where appropriate, measures against data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples, confidentiality attacks and model flaws. Accuracy levels and metrics must be declared in the instructions for use.
provisions.responsible_party: AI provider (of high-risk AI systems)
provisions.applicability_status: Legally adopted but not yet applicable
provisions.implementation_notes: QUALIFIER: legislative obligation. Not assessed: legislative obligation, not a policy commitment. Timing is recorded in applicability_status. Check separately whether harmonised standards supporting this article have been published. APPLICABILITY: from 2 Dec 2027 (Art. 6(2)/Annex III systems) or 2 Aug 2028 (Art. 6(1)/Annex I systems), per Art. 113 as amended. Provider duty; not applicable to AI systems that are not high-risk.
provisions.enforcement_mechanism: Art. 16(a) (cons. p. 28; OJ p. 62) obliges providers to ensure compliance with Chapter III Section 2 (Arts 8-15). Non-compliance with Art. 16 provider obligations is subject to fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher (Art. 99(4)(a), cons. p. 116; OJ p. 115; unchanged by 2026/1744). Ex ante conformity assessment (Art. 43, cons. p. 53); market surveillance (Art. 74, cons. p. 91) and procedure for AI systems presenting a risk (Art. 79, cons. p. 104).
provisions.source_reference: Consolidated text (27.07.2026): https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/2026-07-27/eng/pdf (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/2026-07-27); Original act: OJ L, 2024/1689, 12.7.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj; Amending act: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of 8 July 2026, OJ L, 2026/1744, 24.7.2026, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj
provisions.verification_notes: Binding requirement, but the standard is open-textured ('appropriate level'; 'as resilient as possible'; measures 'where appropriate'), so in practice compliance will be specified through harmonised standards and benchmarks. Art. 15(2) is a separate INSTITUTIONAL duty on the Commission to encourage benchmarks and measurement methodologies. It is not counted in this record and could form a separate record (obligation_type = Institutional). Art. 15(3) (declared accuracy levels and metrics) is included in the coded range; it links to Transparency (Art. 13(3)(b)(ii)) but is not double counted. No M1 marker in Art. 15; wording unchanged. APPLICATION DATE: as amended by Reg. (EU) 2026/1744, Art. 113 (cons. p. 128) applies Chapter III high-risk obligations from 2 Dec 2027 for systems classified under Art. 6(2) and Annex III, and from 2 Aug 2028 for systems classified under Art. 6(1) and Annex I (originally 2 Aug 2026 and 2 Aug 2027 respectively). As of Nov 2026 the obligation is binding law but not yet applicable. provisions.document: India AI Governance Guidelines: Enabling Safe and Trusted AI Innovation (MeitY, IndiaAI Mission, 5 November 2025)
provisions.article_or_section: Part 4 – Practical Guidelines for Industry & Regulators; 'Guidelines for industry', bullet 5 (transparency reports)
provisions.exact_text: Publish transparency reports that evaluate the risk of harm to individuals and society in the Indian context.
provisions.provision_summary: Anyone developing or deploying AI systems in India is advised to publish transparency reports that assess the risk of harm their systems pose to individuals and society in the Indian context. Where a report contains sensitive or proprietary information, it should be shared confidentially with the relevant regulators instead of published.
provisions.responsible_party: Developer and deployer ('any person involved in developing or deploying AI systems in India')
provisions.applicability_status: Not legally binding (policy or international instrument)
provisions.implementation_notes: COMMITMENT: voluntary transparency reports by developers/deployers; MeitY 'may publish a schedule' for compliance within 9-12 months (PDF p. 33). IMPLEMENTATION: no MeitY compliance schedule or transparency-reporting template found as of 25 Nov 2026. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence; check indiaai.gov.in and meity.gov.in.
provisions.enforcement_mechanism: No specific mechanism identified in the examined provision. The Guidelines rely on soft accountability mechanisms (public and peer scrutiny of transparency reports, self-certification, peer monitoring, committee hearings; §2.5, PDF p. 33). MeitY 'may publish a schedule' for compliance with these measures within 9-12 months (PDF p. 33). Voluntary measures may later become mandatory baseline requirements enforced by regulators (§2.4, PDF p. 29).
provisions.source_reference: Official IndiaAI portal: https://indiaai.gov.in/ ; official release: PIB press release, 5 Nov 2025, https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2186639 (links to the report)
provisions.verification_notes: Policy recommendation, not a directly enforceable obligation: Part 4 is introduced as what developers/deployers 'should be guided by'. Related provisions not double counted: Sutra 6 'Understandable by Design' (Part 1, PDF p. 15) and §2.5 'Transparency' about the AI value chain for regulators (PDF p. 35). COMPARISON NOTE: unlike EU AI Act Art. 13 (provider-to-deployer instructions), this is a public or regulator-facing risk-reporting expectation. Check whether MeitY has published the compliance schedule mentioned on PDF p. 33. STATUS: the Guidelines are a drafting-committee report released by MeitY. They create no legal obligations. They expressly state that, at this stage, a separate AI law is not needed and that existing laws (IT Act, data protection, consumer protection, criminal law) should govern AI (Overview, PDF p. 12 / printed p. 10). PAGE NUMBERS: 'PDF p.' is the page in the downloaded file; 'printed p.' is the number printed on the page (printed = PDF - 2). SOURCE URL: confirm the exact report PDF link on indiaai.gov.in; the PIB release points there.

provisions.document: India AI Governance Guidelines: Enabling Safe and Trusted AI Innovation (MeitY, IndiaAI Mission, 5 November 2025)
provisions.article_or_section: Part 2, §2.5 Accountability – Recommendations, bullet 2 (proportionate obligations across the AI value chain); read with 'Liability' (graded liability)
provisions.exact_text: Impose obligations for each of these entities that are proportionate to their function and the risk of harm
provisions.provision_summary: The Guidelines recommend clarifying how each actor in the AI value chain (developers, deployers, end-users) is governed under existing law such as the IT Act, and then imposing obligations on each that match its function and the risk of harm (for example transparency reporting, content removal, grievance redressal and legal assistance). This rests on a 'graded liability' model in which responsibility depends on the function performed, the level of risk and whether due diligence was done.
provisions.responsible_party: Government (MeitY and sectoral regulators) to clarify and impose obligations; the eventual duty-bearers would be developers, deployers and end-users
provisions.applicability_status: Not legally binding (policy or international instrument)
provisions.implementation_notes: COMMITMENT: clarify how value-chain actors are governed and impose proportionate obligations; Action Plan: 'Develop clear liability regimes' (short term). IMPLEMENTATION: no liability regime or AI-specific obligations enacted. Secondary reports (Business Standard, Apr 2026; Economic Times via letsdatascience, Jul 2026) say AIGEG may push a unified legal framework and that MeitY is weighing a risk-based AI law. That would contradict the Guidelines' position that no separate AI law is needed. Unconfirmed; check for a draft bill. Sources: https://www.business-standard.com/industry/news/govt-body-plans-legal-framework-for-ai-companies-tech-oversight-126042001135_1.html ; https://letsdatascience.com/news/india-weighs-dedicated-risk-based-ai-regulation-af49db26
provisions.enforcement_mechanism: No specific mechanism identified in the examined provision; the obligations themselves do not yet exist. Enforcement of existing laws is to be 'timely and consistent' (§2.5 Recommendations, PDF p. 35). Part 3 Action Plan lists 'Develop clear liability regimes across the AI value chain' as a short-term action (PDF p. 40).
provisions.source_reference: Official IndiaAI portal: https://indiaai.gov.in/ ; official release: PIB press release, 5 Nov 2025, https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2186639 (links to the report)
provisions.verification_notes: A recommendation that government should create future obligations; it imposes nothing itself. Record as Recommended with responsible party = Government. Do not count it as an obligation on developers until implemented in law. The RBI FREE-AI Committee's 'tolerant' stance on first-time aberrations is noted but not endorsed as a general rule; the Committee says the rule of law is paramount (PDF p. 34). Related, not double counted: Sutra 5 Accountability (PDF p. 15); grievance redressal recommendation 'Mandate grievance redressal mechanisms' (PDF p. 35), which is a candidate for a separate record. STATUS: the Guidelines are a drafting-committee report released by MeitY. They create no legal obligations. They expressly state that, at this stage, a separate AI law is not needed and that existing laws (IT Act, data protection, consumer protection, criminal law) should govern AI (Overview, PDF p. 12 / printed p. 10). PAGE NUMBERS: 'PDF p.' is the page in the downloaded file; 'printed p.' is the number printed on the page (printed = PDF - 2). SOURCE URL: confirm the exact report PDF link on indiaai.gov.in; the PIB release points there.

provisions.document: India AI Governance Guidelines: Enabling Safe and Trusted AI Innovation (MeitY, IndiaAI Mission, 5 November 2025)
provisions.article_or_section: Part 2, §2.4 Risk Mitigation – Recommendations, bullet 1 (India-specific risk assessment and classification framework)
provisions.exact_text: Develop a risk assessment and classification framework that is customised for India’s local context, and accounts for risks to vulnerable groups.
provisions.provision_summary: The Guidelines recommend developing an India-specific framework for assessing and classifying AI risks, based on real-world evidence of harm and reflecting India's social, economic and cultural context, including risks to vulnerable groups such as children and women. Risk mitigation measures would then be applied on the basis of that classification. The Guidelines identify six risk categories: malicious use, bias and discrimination, transparency failures, systemic risks, loss of control, and national security.
provisions.responsible_party: Government (developing body not named in the provision; Action Plan says 'with sectoral inputs'; AISI's listed functions include risk analysis)
provisions.applicability_status: Not legally binding (policy or international instrument)
provisions.implementation_notes: QUALIFIER: related sector-specific instrument. COMMITMENT: an India-specific, economy-wide risk assessment and classification framework (short-term action). IMPLEMENTATION: no general MeitY framework found. RELATED: CERT-In issued 'AI Security Auditing Guidelines' v1.0 (CISG-2026-04) on 4 Nov 2026, with a four-tier risk classification (Low, Moderate, High, Critical) that sets audit depth and frequency (secondary reports). That instrument covers security auditing, not the general framework recommended. Its legal force (guideline vs binding direction) needs verification from the CERT-In text; it is a candidate for a new IND record. PSA's office published a white paper (Jan 2026) proposing a national AI incidents database; no launch found. Sources: https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/CSA_research_note_certin_ai_security_auditing_guidelines_20261106-csa-styled.pdf ; https://www.business-standard.com/india-news/govt-should-consider-national-database-for-ai-incidents-white-paper-126012400322_1.html
provisions.enforcement_mechanism: Not applicable: this is a framework-building task, not a compliance duty. The linked AI incidents database (recommendation 2, PDF p. 32) is designed to encourage reporting 'without the threat of penalties' (PDF p. 29) and would feed evidence into the framework.

provisions.verification_notes: Short-term action item in Part 3 ('Develop India-specific AI risk assessment and classification frameworks with sectoral inputs', PDF p. 40). provisions.document: India AI Governance Guidelines: Enabling Safe and Trusted AI Innovation (MeitY, IndiaAI Mission, 5 November 2025)
provisions.article_or_section: Part 2, §2.6 Institutions – B. AI Safety Institute (functions)
provisions.exact_text: It should test and evaluate AI systems for risks and provide advice to policymakers and industry actors on issues of AI safety.
provisions.provision_summary: The AI Safety Institute (AISI) is to be the main body guiding safe and trusted AI in India. It should test and evaluate AI systems for risks and advise policymakers and industry on AI safety. It should also develop draft guidelines, standards, evaluation metrics and testing frameworks with relevant agencies, and promote safety tools for bias mitigation, fairness testing and explainability. The related recommendation asks for adequate resources for AISI to develop testing methods and benchmarks.
provisions.responsible_party: AI Safety Institute (IndiaAI Safety Institute), working with agencies and sectoral regulators
provisions.applicability_status: Not legally binding (policy or international instrument)
provisions.implementation_notes: QUALIFIER: institution exists; testing function not verified. COMMITMENT: AISI should test and evaluate AI systems and be adequately resourced. IMPLEMENTATION: IndiaAI Safety Institute announced Jan 2025 under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted pillar, on a hub-and-spoke model; IndiaAI states it 'has been established'. Its published mandate emphasises R&D on tools, benchmarks and measurement. No evidence found of AISI testing or evaluating specific AI systems, or of any power to compel testing. Sources: https://indiaai.gov.in/article/call-for-partnerships-as-part-of-the-indiaai-safety-institute ; https://indiaai.gov.in/article/india-takes-the-lead-establishing-the-indiaai-safety-institute-for-responsible-ai-innovation
provisions.enforcement_mechanism: No specific mechanism identified. AISI's role is research, testing and advice; the Guidelines give it no powers to compel testing or impose sanctions. It provides risk assessments and 'updates on industry compliance' to TPEC and AIGG (PDF p. 38).

provisions.document: India AI Governance Guidelines: Enabling Safe and Trusted AI Innovation (MeitY, IndiaAI Mission, 5 November 2025)
provisions.article_or_section: Part 2, §2.6 Institutions – whole-of-government approach, bullet 1 (sectoral regulators lead on enforcement)
provisions.exact_text: The relevant sectoral agencies and regulators should take the lead in monitoring harms, providing guidance and enforcing regulations in their respective domains.
provisions.provision_summary: Enforcement is left to existing sectoral agencies and regulators, each within its own domain; for example, the Ministry of Finance and RBI for financial services. MeitY is the nodal ministry for AI adoption and regulation. A new AI Governance Group (AIGG), supported by a Technology & Policy Expert Committee (TPEC), is to coordinate policy across ministries, but it is a coordinating body, not an enforcement authority.
provisions.responsible_party: Sectoral regulators and agencies (e.g. RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, TRAI, ICMR, NHA, ministries), with MeitY as nodal ministry and AIGG coordinating
provisions.applicability_status: Not legally binding (policy or international instrument)
provisions.implementation_notes: QUALIFIER: coordinating body established in modified form. COMMITMENT: sectoral regulators enforce within their domains; new AIGG chaired by the PSA, including regulators (TRAI, CCI, DPB, RBI, SEBI etc.), supported by TPEC. IMPLEMENTATION: MeitY Office Memorandum of 13 Apr 2026 constituted the AI Governance and Economic Group (AIGEG), merging the proposed AIGG with the Economic Survey's AI Economic Council. It is chaired by the Minister of Electronics & IT (not the PSA), and none of RBI, SEBI, TRAI, CCI or DPB is a member. Its ToR repeat the Guidelines' AIGG functions and add labour-market tasks. It has no enforcement powers; it was created by an administrative memorandum, not a statute. TPEC constituted (NeGD release, May 2026). Sectoral enforcement continues under existing statutes; no change found. Sources: https://d12aarmt01l54a.cloudfront.net/cms/files/constitution-of-aigeg/1776346498.pdf ; https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2252739 ; https://negd.gov.in/?p=12809
provisions.enforcement_mechanism: Existing statutory powers of sectoral regulators under their own laws; no new AI-specific sanctions or enforcement powers are created. The institutional framework maps regulators to 'Enforcing applicable laws and regulations', 'Supervising compliance' and 'Handling grievances' (PDF pp. 42-43). AIGG is to 'issue guidelines to ensure that firms are held accountable for compliance with local laws' (PDF p. 36).

provisions.document: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation (DSIT White Paper, CP 815, March 2023; amended version)
provisions.article_or_section: Part 3, §3.2.3 A principles-based approach – Principle: Appropriate transparency and explainability
provisions.exact_text: AI systems should be appropriately transparent and explainable.
provisions.provision_summary: AI systems should be transparent and explainable to a degree proportionate to their risk. Transparency means communicating appropriate information about an AI system (how, when and for what it is used); explainability means relevant parties can access, interpret and understand its decision-making. Regulators should have enough information to give effect to the other principles. Affected parties should be able to get enough information to enforce their rights. Regulators may ask life cycle actors to provide information in a required form, including through product labelling.
provisions.responsible_party: Regulatory authority (implementation through guidance); AI life cycle actors (may be asked by regulators to provide information)
provisions.applicability_status: Not legally binding (policy or international instrument)
provisions.implementation_notes: QUALIFIER: non-statutory. COMMITMENT (2023): regulators apply the principle, supported by central guidance. IMPLEMENTATION: the Feb 2024 government response published 'Implementing the UK's AI regulatory principles: initial guidance for regulators' (6 Feb 2024). Ministers asked key regulators for their strategic approaches to AI, which DSIT published on 1 May 2024. The principle remains non-statutory; no standalone UK AI legislation found (law-firm trackers, 2025-2026). Sources: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/implementing-the-uks-ai-regulatory-principles-initial-guidance-for-regulators ; https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/regulators-strategic-approaches-to-ai/regulators-strategic-approaches-to-ai
provisions.enforcement_mechanism: No new enforcement mechanism. The principles are applied by existing regulators 'using the powers and resources available to them' (para 55, PDF p. 41). Government anticipates, but has not committed to, a statutory duty on regulators to 'have due regard' to the principles (para 57, PDF p. 42), and may not introduce it (para 59). Regulators are encouraged to integrate the principles into existing monitoring, investigation and enforcement processes (para 68, PDF p. 46).
provisions.source_reference: GOV.UK publication page: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-regulation-a-pro-innovation-approach ; HTML version: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-regulation-a-pro-innovation-approach/white-paper
provisions.verification_notes: Non-statutory principle; it binds no one directly. Life cycle actors 'may be asked' to provide information, which is conditional on a regulator using existing powers. The White Paper consulted on, but did not adopt, a requirement that organisations disclose when they use AI (consultation Qs 1-2, PDF p. 38; wording corrected by the correction slip, PDF pp. 4-5). The explainability standard is qualified by context, risk and 'what is achievable given the state of the art' (PDF p. 35). STATUS: the White Paper is a policy proposal for consultation. Its principles are 'issued on a non-statutory basis and implemented by existing regulators' (para 11, PDF p. 12). It creates no legal obligations for businesses. Any binding effect comes from regulators' existing statutory powers. LATER DEVELOPMENTS: the Government response to consultation (CP 1019, 6 Feb 2024) kept this approach and should be coded as a separate document if used. It was published under the previous (2022-2024) government; secondary sources indicate no UK AI Act or statutory duty on regulators had been enacted by 2026. Verify on GOV.UK and legislation.gov.uk. PAGE NUMBERS: 'PDF p.' is the page in the downloaded file; 'printed p.' is the number printed on the page (printed = PDF - 6).

provisions.article_or_section: Part 3, §3.2.3 – Principle: Accountability and governance; read with §3.3.2 Government's role in addressing accountability across the life cycle (paras 80-83)
provisions.exact_text: Governance measures should be in place to ensure effective oversight of the supply and use of AI systems, with clear lines of accountability established across the AI life cycle.
provisions.provision_summary: Organisations across the AI life cycle should have governance measures ensuring effective oversight of how AI systems are supplied and used, with clear lines of accountability. Life cycle actors should take steps to follow the principles, and regulators should place clear compliance expectations on the appropriate actors in the supply chain. Regulators may expect documentation of key decisions, impact assessments or audits where appropriate. The White Paper does not change how legal liability is allocated across the life cycle at this stage.

provisions.article_or_section: Part 3, §3.3.1 New central functions – Box 3.1: Cross-sectoral risk assessment (Activities, bullet 1)
provisions.exact_text: Develop and maintain a cross-economy, society-wide AI risk register to support regulators’ internal risks assessments.
provisions.provision_summary: Central government is to run a cross-sectoral risk assessment function. It will develop and maintain an economy-wide AI risk register, monitor and re-prioritise known risks, identify new and emerging risks with the horizon-scanning function, and clarify regulator responsibilities for new or contested risks. It will also identify risks that fall between regulators' remits. The aim is that risks do not fall into gaps and that regulators assess AI risks coherently.

provisions.article_or_section: Part 3, §3.2.3 – Principle: Safety, security and robustness
provisions.exact_text: AI systems should function in a robust, secure and safe way throughout the AI life cycle, and risks should be continually identified, assessed and managed.
provisions.provision_summary: AI systems should be robust, secure and safe throughout their life cycle, and risks should be continually identified, assessed and managed. Regulators may introduce measures so that systems are technically secure and work reliably as intended. Developers should understand security threats at each life cycle stage and build in resilience, with regulators possibly referring to NCSC machine-learning security principles. Regulators' implementation may require life cycle actors to regularly test or carry out due diligence on a system's functioning, resilience and security, and technical standards may serve as benchmarks.

provisions.article_or_section: Part 3, §3.2.4 Our preferred model for applying the principles – para 55 (read with paras 56-59)
provisions.exact_text: Initially, the principles will be issued by government on a non-statutory basis and applied by regulators within their remits.
provisions.provision_summary: Existing regulators apply the five principles within their current remits, using their existing powers and resources, during an initial non-statutory period. After that period, and when parliamentary time allows, the government anticipates introducing a statutory duty requiring regulators to 'have due regard' to the principles. It would not introduce the duty if monitoring shows it is unnecessary. There is no new AI regulator.

provisions.applicability_status: Not legally binding (policy or international instrument)

provisions.document: Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence, OECD/LEGAL/0449 (adopted 22 May 2019; revised 8 November 2023 and 3 May 2024)
provisions.article_or_section: Section 1, Principle 1.3 Transparency and explainability (i)-(iv)
provisions.exact_text: AI Actors should commit to transparency and responsible disclosure regarding AI systems.
provisions.provision_summary: AI actors should commit to transparency and responsible disclosure. They should give meaningful, context-appropriate information so that people understand AI systems' capabilities and limitations, know when they are interacting with AI (including at work), and, where feasible and useful, understand the data, factors and logic behind an output. People adversely affected by an AI system should get information enabling them to challenge its output.
provisions.responsible_party: AI actors (Council 'CALLS ON all AI actors', para III); Adherent governments to promote and implement (para II)
provisions.applicability_status: Not legally binding (policy or international instrument)
provisions.implementation_notes: International principle addressed to Adherents and AI actors; implementation varies by Adherent and is not assessed in this record. See OECD005 for the monitoring mechanism.
provisions.enforcement_mechanism: No enforcement or sanctions. Implementation is monitored through the Digital Policy Committee's reports to Council (Section VIII(d), p. 11), OECD.AI Policy Observatory and practical guidance (see OECD005).
provisions.source_reference: Compendium of OECD Legal Instruments: https://legalinstruments.oecd.org/en/instruments/OECD-LEGAL-0449 ; PDF: https://legalinstruments.oecd.org/public/doc/648/648.en.pdf
provisions.verification_notes: Non-binding principle; addressed both to governments and directly to AI actors. Point (iii) is limited to 'where feasible and useful'. The 2024 revision clarified the information AI actors should provide (Background, p. 4). BENCHMARK USE: compare (ii) awareness of interaction with EU AI Act Art. 50 and the UK consultation question on disclosure. Compare (iv) challenge with the UK contestability principle. STATUS: an OECD Council Recommendation adopted under Art. 5(b) of the OECD Convention (cited in the preamble, p. 7). Recommendations are not legally binding; Adherents make a political commitment to implement them. Not a country; use as a benchmark only. ADHERENCE: UK (OECD Member) and EU adhere. India is not an OECD Member and, to my knowledge, has not adhered. Verify on the 'Adherents' tab of the Compendium page. PAGE NUMBERS: PDF page = printed page.

provisions.document: Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence, OECD/LEGAL/0449 (adopted 22 May 2019; revised 8 November 2023 and 3 May 2024)
provisions.article_or_section: Section 1, Principle 1.5 Accountability, paragraphs (a)-(b)
provisions.exact_text: AI actors should be accountable for the proper functioning of AI systems and for the respect of the above principles, based on their roles, the context, and consistent with the state of the art.
provisions.provision_summary: AI actors should be accountable for the proper functioning of AI systems and for respecting the OECD principles, according to their roles and context. To that end they should ensure traceability of datasets, processes and decisions across the lifecycle, so that outputs can be analysed and inquiries answered.
provisions.responsible_party: AI actors (those playing an active role in the AI system lifecycle, including those who deploy or operate AI; definitions, p. 8)
provisions.applicability_status: Not legally binding (policy or international instrument)
provisions.implementation_notes: International principle addressed to Adherents and AI actors; implementation varies by Adherent and is not assessed in this record. See OECD005 for the monitoring mechanism.
provisions.enforcement_mechanism: No enforcement or sanctions. Implementation is monitored through the Digital Policy Committee's reports to Council (Section VIII(d), p. 11), OECD.AI Policy Observatory and practical guidance (see OECD005).
provisions.source_reference: Compendium of OECD Legal Instruments: https://legalinstruments.oecd.org/en/instruments/OECD-LEGAL-0449 ; PDF: https://legalinstruments.oecd.org/public/doc/648/648.en.pdf
provisions.verification_notes: Non-binding. Principle 1.5 has three paragraphs. (a)-(b) (accountability and traceability) are coded here, and (c) (risk management) is coded separately as OECD003. They are distinct requirements, but OECD002 and OECD003 share one principle; report them as linked in analysis. Human oversight appears in Principle 1.2(b) ('capacity for human agency and oversight', p. 8), not 1.5. Compare with EU AI Act Art. 14 under Accountability; candidate for a later record. STATUS: an OECD Council Recommendation adopted under Art. 5(b) of the OECD Convention (cited in the preamble, p. 7). provisions.document: Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence, OECD/LEGAL/0449 (adopted 22 May 2019; revised 8 November 2023 and 3 May 2024)
provisions.article_or_section: Section 1, Principle 1.5 Accountability, paragraph (c) (systematic risk management)
provisions.exact_text: AI actors, should, based on their roles, the context, and their ability to act, apply a systematic risk management approach to each phase of the AI system lifecycle on an ongoing basis
provisions.provision_summary: AI actors should apply a systematic, ongoing risk management approach to every phase of the AI lifecycle, according to their role, context and ability to act, and adopt responsible business conduct, including by cooperating with suppliers, users and other stakeholders. Risks include harmful bias, human rights (including safety, security and privacy), labour rights and intellectual property rights.
provisions.responsible_party: AI actors, with cooperation among AI actors, suppliers of AI knowledge and resources, AI system users and other stakeholders
provisions.applicability_status: Not legally binding (policy or international instrument)
provisions.implementation_notes: International principle addressed to Adherents and AI actors; implementation varies by Adherent and is not assessed in this record. See OECD005 for the monitoring mechanism.
provisions.enforcement_mechanism: No enforcement or sanctions. Implementation is monitored through the Digital Policy Committee's reports to Council (Section VIII(d), p. 11), OECD.AI Policy Observatory and practical guidance (see OECD005).
provisions.source_reference: Compendium of OECD Legal Instruments: https://legalinstruments.oecd.org/en/instruments/OECD-LEGAL-0449 ; PDF: https://legalinstruments.oecd.org/public/doc/648/648.en.pdf
provisions.verification_notes: Non-binding. LINKED to OECD002 (same principle 1.5); documented to avoid double counting. The 2024 revision moved the text on risk management into the Accountability principle (Background, p. 5). So the OECD treats risk management as part of accountability, a framing difference from the codebook. exact_text is the opening clause of 1.5(c), cut before 'and adopt responsible business conduct'; the original comma after 'AI actors' is kept. COMPARISON NOTE: closest analogue to EU AI Act Art. 9, but with no risk tiers and no addressee beyond 'AI actors'. provisions.document: Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence, OECD/LEGAL/0449 (adopted 22 May 2019; revised 8 November 2023 and 3 May 2024)
provisions.article_or_section: Section 1, Principle 1.4 Robustness, security and safety, paragraphs (a)-(c)
provisions.exact_text: AI systems should be robust, secure and safe throughout their entire lifecycle so that, in conditions of normal use, foreseeable use or misuse, or other adverse conditions, they function appropriately and do not pose unreasonable safety and/or security risks.
provisions.provision_summary: AI systems should be robust, secure and safe throughout their lifecycle, working appropriately and without unreasonable safety or security risks under normal use, foreseeable use or misuse, or adverse conditions. There should be mechanisms to override, repair or safely decommission systems that risk undue harm or behave undesirably. Where technically feasible, there should also be mechanisms to bolster information integrity while respecting freedom of expression.
provisions.responsible_party: Multiple stakeholders (principle phrased in the passive voice; addressed to AI actors via para III and to Adherents via para II)
provisions.applicability_status: Not legally binding (policy or international instrument)
provisions.implementation_notes: International principle addressed to Adherents and AI actors; implementation varies by Adherent and is not assessed in this record. See OECD005 for the monitoring mechanism.
provisions.enforcement_mechanism: No enforcement or sanctions. Implementation is monitored through the Digital Policy Committee's reports to Council (Section VIII(d), p. 11), OECD.AI Policy Observatory and practical guidance (see OECD005).

provisions.verification_notes: Non-binding. The principle does not use the word 'testing'; testing appears in the lifecycle definition ('test, evaluate, verify and validate', p. 8) and in Recommendation 2.3(a) on controlled experimentation environments (p. 10). Coding under Safety and Testing rests on robustness and security. The override/decommission mechanism in (b) was added in the 2024 revision (Background, p. 4). It also has an Accountability dimension (human control, compare EU Art. 14(4)(e)); not double counted. provisions.document: Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence, OECD/LEGAL/0449 (adopted 22 May 2019; revised 8 November 2023 and 3 May 2024)
provisions.article_or_section: Section VIII (instructions to the Digital Policy Committee), point (d); read with points (a)-(c)
provisions.exact_text: report to Council, in consultation with other relevant committees, on the implementation, dissemination and continued relevance of this Recommendation no later than five years following its revision and at least every ten years thereafter.
provisions.provision_summary: The OECD Council instructs its Digital Policy Committee, through the Working Party on AI Governance, to report on how the Recommendation is being implemented, disseminated and kept relevant. Reports are due within five years of the revision and at least every ten years after that. The Committee must also continue its AI work, develop practical implementation guidance and provide a forum for exchanging information (supported by the OECD.AI Policy Observatory).
provisions.responsible_party: OECD Digital Policy Committee, through its Working Party on AI Governance (AIGO)
provisions.applicability_status: Not legally binding (policy or international instrument)
provisions.implementation_notes: COMMITMENT: DPC reports to Council on implementation. IMPLEMENTATION: the 2024 Report to Council was delivered and found the Recommendation 'being implemented by its Adherents' (Recommendation PDF, p. 5). The next report is due no later than five years after the 2024 revision.
provisions.enforcement_mechanism: Periodic reporting to Council and peer exchange only. No sanctions, compliance assessment or dispute mechanism. The 2024 Report to Council found the Recommendation was 'being implemented by its Adherents' (p. 5).
provisions.source_reference: Compendium of OECD Legal Instruments: https://legalinstruments.oecd.org/en/instruments/OECD-LEGAL-0449 ; PDF: https://legalinstruments.oecd.org/public/doc/648/648.en.pdf
provisions.verification_notes: CODING DECISION: the OECD instrument has no enforcement in the legal sense. This record captures its nearest analogue (institutional monitoring of implementation) and documents the absence of enforcement. In analysis, treat it as 'monitoring only'; do not count it as equivalent to EU penalties (Art. 99) or regulator enforcement. Related: Recommendation 2.3(b) asks governments to review and adapt their regulatory frameworks and assessment mechanisms (p. 10), and 2.5(d) asks them to develop indicators to measure implementation (p. 10). Neither is coded separately. exact_text is the operative clause of VIII(d); its subject ('INSTRUCTS the Digital Policy Committee...') is in the chapeau of Section VIII. STATUS: an OECD Council Recommendation adopted under Art. 5(b) of the OECD Convention (cited in the preamble, p. 7). Recommendations are not legally binding; Adherents make a political commitment to implement them. Not a country; use as a benchmark only. ADHERENCE: UK (OECD Member) and EU adhere. India is not an OECD Member and, to my knowledge, has not adhered. Verify on the 'Adherents' tab of the Compendium page. PAGE NUMBERS: PDF page = printed page.
